stem: What is an **alloy**?

options.content: a mixture of a metal with other elements
options.rationale: Usually other metals or carbon.

options.content: a pure metal that has been polished
options.rationale: Polishing does not change the composition.

options.content: an oxide of a metal
options.rationale: A metal oxide is a compound with oxygen.

options.content: a compound of two metals in a fixed ratio
options.rationale: Alloys are mixtures, so their composition can vary.

explanation: An alloy is a mixture of a metal with other elements, such as brass (copper and zinc) or steel (iron and carbon).

stem: Brass is an alloy of copper and which other metal?

options.content: tin
options.rationale: Copper + tin is bronze.

options.content: aluminium
options.rationale: Aluminium is the main metal in duralumin.

options.content: iron
options.rationale: Iron is the main metal in steel.

options.content: zinc
options.rationale: Brass = copper + zinc.

explanation: Brass is a mixture of copper and zinc. It is harder than copper and resists corrosion.

stem: True or false: alloys are often harder and stronger than the pure metals they are made from.

answerSpec.feedbackTrue: Correct: this is why most metal objects are made from alloys.
answerSpec.feedbackFalse: It is true: alloys such as brass and steel are harder and stronger than copper and iron.

explanation: Adding atoms of other elements makes the metal harder and stronger, so alloys are more useful than many pure metals.

stem: Stainless steel is iron mixed with small amounts of other elements. Which elements?

options.content: aluminium and magnesium
options.rationale: These are found in light aluminium alloys, not steel.

options.content: chromium, nickel and carbon
options.rationale: These make the steel hard and resistant to rusting.

options.content: copper and tin
options.rationale: Copper and tin make bronze.

options.content: copper and zinc
options.rationale: Copper and zinc make brass.

explanation: Stainless steel is iron with chromium, nickel and a little carbon. It is hard and does not rust easily.

stem: Why is stainless steel used to make cutlery?

options.content: It is a good electrical conductor.
options.rationale: Conductivity is not needed for cutlery.

options.content: It is hard and resists rusting.
options.rationale: Knives keep their edge and the cutlery stays shiny when washed.

options.content: It has a very low density.
options.rationale: Stainless steel is quite dense; low density is not the reason.

options.content: It is soft and easily bent.
options.rationale: Cutlery must be hard.

explanation: Cutlery is used with water and food acids. Stainless steel is hard and resists rusting, so it lasts and stays clean.

stem: Match each alloy with the main elements it contains.
explanation: Brass: copper + zinc. Bronze: copper + tin. Stainless steel: iron + chromium + nickel (+ carbon). Duralumin: aluminium + copper (+ small amounts of magnesium and manganese). Iron coated with zinc is galvanised iron, not an alloy.

stem: Why is an alloy usually **harder** than the pure metal?

options.content: An alloy contains fewer delocalised electrons, so the ions repel more.
options.rationale: The reason is the distortion of the layers, not fewer electrons.

options.content: The alloy is a compound with a fixed formula.
options.rationale: An alloy is a mixture.

options.content: Different-sized atoms disrupt the layers, so they cannot slide easily.
options.rationale: More force is needed to change the shape.

options.content: The atoms of the two metals form strong covalent bonds with each other.
options.rationale: The bonding in an alloy is still metallic.

explanation: In a pure metal, identical atoms form regular layers that slide easily. In an alloy, different-sized atoms distort the layers, so they cannot slide easily: the alloy is harder and stronger.
hints: Think about what happens to the layers in a pure metal when it is bent.

stem: Four particle diagrams are described in words. Which one represents an **alloy**?

options.content: identical circles in rows, with some replaced by larger circles
options.rationale: Different-sized atoms are mixed into the metal lattice.

options.content: pairs of joined circles, far apart and randomly arranged
options.rationale: This is a gas made of diatomic molecules.

options.content: a block of large circles next to a separate block of small circles
options.rationale: The two elements are side by side, not mixed, so this is not an alloy.

options.content: identical circles in neat, regular rows with no gaps
options.rationale: This is a pure metal.

explanation: An alloy diagram shows a mainly regular arrangement of one kind of atom with some atoms of a different size mixed among them.
hints: An alloy is a mixture at the level of atoms.

stem: Name the alloy made mainly of copper and tin.

rejected.feedback: Brass is copper and zinc. Copper and tin make bronze.
Solder is mainly tin (with lead or copper).

explanation: Bronze is copper mixed with tin. It is hard and resists corrosion, so it is used for statues, medals and bells.

stem: A brass key has a mass of 12.0 g. It contains 7.8 g of copper; the rest is zinc. Calculate the percentage by mass of zinc in the key.
explanation: Mass of zinc $= 12.0 - 7.8 = 4.2\ \text{g}$. Percentage $= \dfrac{4.2}{12.0} \times 100 = 35.0\%$.
hints: Find the mass of zinc first.

stem:
Thandeka compares the hardness of four metal samples. She drops a steel ball from the same height onto a flat sample of each and measures the diameter of the dent it makes.

| Sample | copper | brass | aluminium | duralumin |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Diameter of dent / mm | 4.2 | 2.6 | 4.8 | 2.9 |

options.content: copper
options.rationale: Copper has a larger dent than brass.

options.content: aluminium
options.rationale: Aluminium has the largest dent: it is the softest.

options.content: brass
options.rationale: The smallest dent shows the hardest metal.

options.content: duralumin
options.rationale: Duralumin is hard, but its dent is slightly larger than brass's.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: What conclusion can be drawn from the results?

options.content: Aluminium is harder than copper, the other pure metal.
options.rationale: Aluminium made a larger dent than copper.

options.content: Hardness does not depend on composition.
options.rationale: The alloys and pure metals gave very different dents.

options.content: Each alloy is harder than the pure metal it is mainly made of.
options.rationale: Brass is harder than copper, and duralumin is harder than aluminium.

options.content: Pure metals are harder than the alloys made from them.
options.rationale: The pure metals made the larger dents.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Explain, in terms of particles, why brass is harder than copper.

points.description: Brass contains zinc atoms of a different size from the copper atoms
which disrupt the layers so they cannot slide over each other easily

parts.explanation: In pure copper, identical atoms form regular layers that slide easily. In brass, the zinc atoms are a different size; they distort the layers so that the layers cannot slide easily, making brass harder.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: State **two** things Thandeka must keep the same to make the test fair.

points.description: The same thickness/shape of sample (any two)

parts.explanation: She must use the same steel ball, drop it from the same height and use samples of the same thickness.

explanation: A smaller dent means a harder metal. Brass (2.6 mm) is harder than copper (4.2 mm), and duralumin (2.9 mm) is harder than aluminium (4.8 mm): alloys are harder because different-sized atoms stop the layers sliding.
hints: A harder metal makes a smaller dent.

stem: Why is duralumin, rather than pure aluminium, used for aircraft bodies?

options.content: It has a much higher density.
options.rationale: A high density would make the aircraft heavy.

options.content: It conducts electricity better than aluminium.
options.rationale: Conductivity is not what an aircraft body needs.

options.content: It is a pure element, so it does not corrode.
options.rationale: Duralumin is an alloy, not a pure element.

options.content: It is much stronger, but its density is still low.
options.rationale: Aircraft need light, strong materials.

explanation: Pure aluminium is light but weak. Adding copper (and a little magnesium and manganese) makes duralumin, which is much stronger while staying light.
hints: Aircraft need two properties at once.

stem: Bronze is used for statues and medals that stand outdoors for many years. Which properties make it suitable?

options.content: It is a good conductor of electricity.
options.rationale: Conductivity is not needed for a statue.

options.content: It has a low melting point, so it melts in the sun.
options.rationale: A statue must not melt.

options.content: It is hard and resists corrosion.
options.rationale: Bronze keeps its shape and does not corrode away in rain.

options.content: It is soft, so it can be shaped by hand.
options.rationale: Bronze is cast or worked with tools; it is hard.

explanation: Bronze (copper and tin) is hard, strong and resists corrosion, so outdoor bronze objects last a very long time.
hints: What happens to metals left outside in the rain?

stem: Ordinary steel is an alloy of iron and which element?

options.content: copper
options.rationale: Copper is the main metal in brass and bronze.

options.content: tin
options.rationale: Tin is used in bronze and for coating ('tin') cans.

options.content: zinc
options.rationale: Zinc is used to galvanise iron, as a coating, not as an alloying element in ordinary steel.

options.content: carbon
options.rationale: Steel is iron with a small percentage of carbon.

explanation: Steel is iron mixed with a small amount of carbon; it is much harder and stronger than pure iron.

stem: Complete the sentences about alloys.

payload.template: Brass is a mixture of copper and {{blank:a}}. Stainless steel is iron mixed with elements such as {{blank:b}}, nickel and carbon. Alloys are often {{blank:c}} than the pure metals.

explanation: Brass = copper + zinc. Stainless steel = iron + chromium, nickel and carbon. Alloys can be harder and stronger than pure metals.

stem: Explain why pure iron is soft but steel, an alloy of iron with carbon, is hard. You may describe what a diagram would show. [4]

points.description: In pure iron, all the atoms are the same size and arranged in regular layers
The layers can slide over each other easily when a force is applied, so iron is soft
In steel, carbon atoms (of a different size) are mixed in among the iron atoms
They disrupt the layers, so the layers cannot slide easily and steel is harder

answerSpec.modelAnswer: In pure iron all the atoms are the same size and are packed in regular layers. When a force is applied, the layers slide over each other easily, so pure iron is soft. In steel, smaller carbon atoms sit among the iron atoms. They disrupt the regular layers, so the layers cannot slide over each other easily, and more force is needed to change the shape: steel is harder and stronger.

explanation: Different-sized atoms distort the layers of metal atoms and stop them sliding, which is why alloys are harder.
hints: Compare what the layers of atoms can do in each.

stem: Which observation shows that brass is a **mixture**, not a compound, of copper and zinc?

options.content: Brass can be made with different percentages of zinc.
options.rationale: A compound has a fixed composition; a mixture can vary.

options.content: Brass is harder than the copper it is made from.
options.rationale: Hardness does not show whether it is a mixture or a compound.

options.content: Brass is shiny and yellow, unlike copper or zinc.
options.rationale: Appearance does not show whether it is a mixture.

options.content: Brass conducts electricity, as copper and zinc do.
options.rationale: Many compounds and mixtures conduct; this does not tell them apart.

explanation: The proportions of the elements in a compound are fixed. Brass can contain anything from about 5% to over 40% zinc, so it is a mixture (an alloy).
hints: What is always true about the composition of a compound?

stem: A stainless-steel fork stamped "18/8" contains 18% chromium and 8% nickel by mass; assume the rest is iron. The fork has a mass of 150 g. Calculate the mass of iron in the fork.
explanation: Percentage of iron $= 100 - 18 - 8 = 74\%$. Mass of iron $= 0.74 \times 150 = 111\ \text{g}$.
hints: Subtract the chromium and nickel percentages from 100%.

stem: Pure gold is described as 24-carat. A ring made of 18-carat gold contains 18 parts gold in every 24 parts by mass; the rest is a mixture of copper and silver.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: The ring has a mass of 4.20 g. Calculate the mass of gold in the ring.
parts.workedSolution:
1. Fraction of gold $= \dfrac{18}{24} = 0.75$.
2. Mass of gold $= 0.75 \times 4.20 = 3.15\ \text{g}$.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Suggest why 18-carat gold is used for rings rather than pure gold.

options.content: Pure gold corrodes in air.
options.rationale: Pure gold does not corrode.

options.content: The alloy is a better conductor of electricity than gold.
options.rationale: Conductivity is not important for a ring.

options.content: Pure gold is too hard to shape into a thin ring.
options.rationale: Pure gold is very soft and malleable.

options.content: The alloy is harder, so the ring does not bend or scratch.
options.rationale: Copper and silver atoms disrupt the gold layers.

explanation: $\dfrac{18}{24} = 75\%$ gold, so the ring contains $0.75 \times 4.20 = 3.15\ \text{g}$ of gold. Pure gold is very soft; alloying it with copper and silver makes it harder, so the ring keeps its shape.
hints: 18 out of 24 parts is what percentage?

stem: True or false: an alloy is a compound of two or more metals.

answerSpec.feedbackTrue: Not quite: an alloy is a mixture. Its composition can vary, and it may contain a non-metal such as carbon.
answerSpec.feedbackFalse: Correct: an alloy is a mixture of a metal with other elements, not a compound.

explanation: An alloy is a mixture of a metal with other elements (metals or non-metals such as carbon). The elements are not chemically combined in a fixed ratio.

stem: Why are many pure metals too soft for uses such as tools and building frames?

options.content: Their atoms are held together by weak covalent bonds.
options.rationale: Metals have metallic bonding.

options.content: Their layers of identical atoms slide over each other easily.
options.rationale: This is why pure metals bend and dent easily.

options.content: They have no delocalised electrons to hold them.
options.rationale: All metals have delocalised electrons.

options.content: They melt at room temperature.
options.rationale: Only mercury is liquid at room temperature.

explanation: In a pure metal the atoms are all the same size, so the layers slide easily when a force is applied. Alloying stops this and makes the metal harder.
hints: Think about the arrangement of atoms in a pure metal.
